name: Khartoum
info: Khartoum is the capital of Sudan, at the confluence of the Blue Nile and the White Nile, founded in 1821 as an Egyptian army outpost and later the seat of Egyptian and Anglo-Egyptian rule in Sudan.

facts.founded: Established in 1821, 24 km north of the ancient city of Soba, by Isma'il Kamil Pasha, third son of Egypt's ruler Muhammad Ali Pasha, as an outpost for the Egyptian Army.
facts.where: At the confluence of the Blue Nile and the White Nile in central Sudan, at an elevation of 385 m, with Khartoum North and Omdurman across the rivers.
facts.known: The Egyptian colonial capital from 1823; a centre of caravan trade and the slave trade; the siege of 1884 to 1885 and the death of General Gordon; the Anglo-Egyptian capital rebuilt after 1898; the capital of independent Sudan from 1956
facts.today: Khartoum is the capital of Sudan and of Khartoum State, and with Khartoum North and Omdurman forms the country's largest urban area.

t: Khartoum was founded in 1821 as an Egyptian army outpost and became the seat of the colonial government in 1823, a trading town on the caravan route from Ethiopia to Egypt and a focal point of the slave trade.

Mahdist forces besieged it from 13 March 1884 and took it on 26 January 1885, after which it was largely destroyed and abandoned, and Anglo-Egyptian forces refounded it as a capital after the reconquest of 1898.

It became the capital of independent Sudan in 1956, grew from 185,000 people in 1964 to an estimated 7.1 million in Greater Khartoum, and saw extensive fighting between the armed forces and the Rapid Support Forces from 2023.
dyk: After the Mahdists took Khartoum in 1885 the survivors were deported to the newly established Omdurman, and when the city was rebuilt after 1898 its street plan was laid out in the shape of the Union Jack.
ev: Isma'il Kamil Pasha establishes Khartoum as an outpost of the Egyptian Army
Egypt moves the seat of its colonial government from Wad Madani to Khartoum
Heavy rains and floods destroy most of the city, which is rebuilt in mud and stone
The Mahdists take Khartoum after a siege that began in 1884, and the garrison is annihilated
Anglo-Egyptian forces reoccupy the city, which becomes the capital of Anglo-Egyptian Sudan
Khartoum becomes the capital of independent Sudan
Fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces begins in the city

sections.origins:
Khartoum stands where the White Nile, flowing north from Lake Victoria, meets the Blue Nile, flowing west from Lake Tana in Ethiopia. The place where the two rivers join is known as al-Mogran or al-Muqran, 'The Confluence'. The land is relatively flat, at an elevation of 385 m, and the climate is a hot desert one: average annual rainfall is only 121.3 mm, and the brief rainy season has its maximum in August. The rivers divide the metropolitan area into three parts, Khartoum proper, Khartoum North to the east and Omdurman to the west, which are linked by bridges.

In 1821 Khartoum was established 24 km north of the ancient city of Soba by Isma'il Kamil Pasha, the third son of Egypt's ruler Muhammad Ali Pasha, who had just incorporated Sudan into his realm. It began as an outpost for the Egyptian Army. In 1823 Egypt shifted the seat of its colonial government from Wad Madani to Khartoum, which became a permanent settlement. The origin of the name is uncertain. One folk etymology derives it from the Arabic khurṭūm, 'trunk' or 'hose', probably for the narrow strip of land between the two Niles; Captain J. A. Grant, who reached the city in 1863, thought it came from qurṭum, 'safflower'; and other proposals are the Nubian Agartum and the Beja hartoom, 'meeting'.
sections.growth:
With its elevation to capital status Khartoum grew quickly into a regional centre of trade, serving as a rest area on the caravan route from Ethiopia to Egypt. It was also a major focal point of the slave trade. The British explorer Samuel Baker, who visited in 1862, called slavery the industry 'that kept Khartoum going as a bustling town'. Under European pressure Egypt closed the city's public slave market in 1854, although slaves continued to be sold and trafficked in large numbers, from the Blue Nile region and the Nuba Mountains and down the White Nile from Dinka and Shilluk territories. Khartoum also became the seat of several European consulates and of the Apostolic Vicariate of Central Africa.

After 1898 the city grew rapidly under British administration. The Gordon Memorial College, now the University of Khartoum, opened in 1903, and a new railway to Port Sudan was completed in 1919. These developments prompted large migration from rural areas, and by 1930 Khartoum was estimated to have more than 50,000 people. Growth continued after independence. The population rose to 185,000 by 1964 and stood at 334,000 in the census of 1973. The first oil pipeline between Khartoum and Port Sudan was completed in 1977.
sections.rulers:
Khartoum was founded while Sudan was part of the realm of Egypt's ruler Muhammad Ali Pasha, and from 1823 it was the seat of Egypt's colonial government. In 1882 the British Empire took control of the Egyptian government, leaving the administration of Sudan in the hands of the Egyptians. At the outbreak of the Mahdist War the British attempted to evacuate the Anglo-Egyptian garrisons from Sudan, and Khartoum fell to the forces of the Mahdi, Muhammad Ahmad, in January 1885. The city was then largely abandoned, and the Mahdists made the newly established Omdurman their centre.

The reconquest of Sudan by Anglo-Egyptian forces in 1898 made Khartoum the capital of Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, and it remained the seat of that government until 1956. Herbert Kitchener became Governor-General in September 1898 and began a programme of reconstruction, and Reginald Wingate held the office from 1899 to 1916. In 1956 the city was designated the capital of an independent Sudan. A military coup on 26 October 2021 left at least 7 dead, and Prime Minister Abdalla Hamdok was arrested and held with other cabinet members in an unknown location.
sections.life:
Under the Egyptians Khartoum became a town of mud and stone houses, which replaced houses of thatch and straw after the floods of 1854. After 1898 Kitchener ordered the mosques rebuilt and guaranteed freedom of religion to all citizens, and he prevented Christian missionaries from trying to proselytise the local Muslims. The new Khartoum was laid out on a street plan in the shape of the Union Jack. Its buildings were modelled on Victorian architecture, with a distinct Middle Eastern influence and Mediterranean-style windows and balconies, and Wingate rebuilt the Governor-General's Palace in red brick with sandstone corners. Khartoum North was established as a garrison with a dockyard and a railhead to Egypt, while Omdurman remained the most populous part and largely kept its old shape.

In the 1970s and 1980s hundreds of thousands of refugees came to Khartoum from Chad, Eritrea, Ethiopia and Uganda. Many Eritrean and Ethiopian refugees assimilated, while others settled in large slums on the outskirts, and since the mid-1980s large numbers from South Sudan and Darfur have settled around the city. The Souq al Arabi, spread over several blocks south of the Great Mosque, is its largest open-air market. Mosques predominate among its places of worship, alongside Coptic Orthodox, Roman Catholic, Greek Orthodox, Presbyterian and other churches. The National Museum of Sudan, founded in 1971, holds two Egyptian temples, those of Buhen and Semna, moved to Khartoum when Lake Nasser flooded their sites.
sections.crises:
In 1854 heavy rains and floods destroyed most of the city. On 13 March 1884 troops loyal to the Mahdi Muhammad Ahmad began the siege of Khartoum against the Egyptian garrison led by the British General Charles George Gordon. The city was fortified by trenches and by a wall connecting the Blue and White Niles, but the Mahdists conquered it on 26 January 1885 and the entire garrison was annihilated. Many of the inhabitants were massacred or enslaved, the survivors were deported to Omdurman, and Khartoum was largely destroyed and abandoned.

In 1973 members of Black September held 10 hostages at the Saudi Arabian embassy, five of them diplomats; the US ambassador, the US deputy ambassador and the Belgian chargé d'affaires were murdered. In November 1991 the government of President Omar al-Bashir sought to remove half the city's population, mostly southern Sudanese deemed squatters; about 425,000 people were placed in five 'Peace Camps' in the desert. On 3 June 2019 the Khartoum massacre took place: over 100 dissidents were killed by soldiers of the Rapid Support Forces, or 61 by the government's count, during protests calling for a civilian government.

On 15 April 2023 fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the RSF broke out across Sudan, including in Khartoum, at the presidential palace, the RSF's headquarters and the airport. The Sudanese Armed Forces regained full control of the city on 26 March 2025, leaving widespread destruction.
sections.legacy:
Khartoum was largely destroyed in 1885, and what stands from the next period includes the street plan, the rebuilt mosques, the Governor-General's Palace and Gordon Memorial College, now the University of Khartoum. Its architecture reflects the history of the city since the early 1820s and is marked by native Sudanese, Turkish, British and modern buildings. The Republican Palace Museum stands in the former Anglican All Saints' cathedral beside the old Presidential Palace, and the National Botanical Garden in the Mogran district is one of the oldest in Africa.

As capital of independent Sudan, Khartoum hosted the Organization of African Unity summit of 18 to 22 July 1978, the African Union summit of January 2006 and the Arab League summit of March 2006. In July 2020 activists demanded that al-Zibar Basha street be renamed, after al-Zubayr Rahma Mansur, a slave trader; the street leads to the military base where the 2019 massacre took place. Literary works and Arabic poetry have taken the city's movement, political instability and social change as their subject.

Khartoum is today the capital and most populous city of Sudan and of Khartoum State. With Khartoum North and Omdurman it forms Greater Khartoum, the largest urban area in Sudan, with an estimated population of 7.1 million people.

summary: Khartoum, at the meeting of the Blue and White Niles, was founded in 1821 as an Egyptian army outpost. It fell to the Mahdists in 1885, was rebuilt as the capital of Anglo-Egyptian Sudan after 1898, and became the capital of independent Sudan in 1956.
notes: Only wp/khartoum.txt exists (no history article). It gives the 1898 reconquest in one clause and describes no battle (Omdurman is named only as the place survivors were deported to in 1885 and as the most populous part of the later city), so the 1898 battle is not told; I could only say Anglo-Egyptian forces reconquered Sudan in 1898.
FOUNDER: the lead says founded by Muhammad Ali Pasha; the History says established by Isma'il Kamil Pasha, his third son. I wrote the History's version and named the father as ruler.

Khartoum massacre: the article says over 100 killed, the government 61, 70 women raped; I gave 100 and 61 and left out the rape figure and any verdict. Count wording 'according to the article's count' in crises should be changed to 'estimates' by the editor if it reads as speaking of the source.

Left out: the 1973 declassified State Department conclusion about Arafat (an attributed verdict); the 2005 riots after Garang's death; the 2012 Yarmouk factory explosion; the 2007-2008 development projects; hotels, malls, airport, clubs (guide rules); Syrian population (given 'as of 2019').
1991 Peace Camps: described as the article does ('sought to remove half the population', residents 'deemed squatters'); no claim about intent beyond that.
The 2021 coup is told as dated fact in 'rulers'. The Mahdist take-over date 26 January 1885 and 'January 1885' consistent.
The 2023 war and the 2025 recapture are given as bare dated facts; 'leaving widespread destruction' is the lead's wording.
Population 7.1 million is the lead's 'estimated' figure, undated in the article.
